title: Tier 3: Abstract (~10–25 years)

html: This is the next major restructuring: the child’s coordinated representational systems are internalized into stable abstractions-intangible, generalizable concepts that transcend any particular concrete instance. Where representational thought remained anchored to specific objects, events, or roles (this doctor, that act of sharing, my mother’s anger yesterday), abstract thought captures what is common across many such instances, yielding concepts like "honesty," "justice," or "addition" as a general operation rather than a collection of specific arithmetic facts. Fischer emphasizes that at this point individuals can reason about hypothetical and counterfactual situations, manipulating ideas that have never been directly experienced and may never exist in concrete form. A paradigmatic example is the emergence of abstract moral concepts: rather than simply knowing that "sharing my toy with Sam was nice" and "hitting my sister was mean," the young adolescent can now grasp "fairness" as a general principle-an invisible entity that organizes and explains diverse concrete situations without being reducible to any one of them.
